topic: Getting up off the floor: a skill worth practising

slides.headline: Can you get up off the floor easily?
slides.sub: It's a skill, and like any skill it improves with practice.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Playing with grandkids, stretching on a mat, or getting up after a slip all need this skill. Practising it builds leg strength, balance and the confidence to get down there at all.

slides.title: Break it into steps
slides.body: From lying, roll to your side, push up onto hands and knees, bring one foot forward into a half kneel, then push up through that leg. Use a chair or couch for support to start.

slides.title: Practise both ways
slides.body: Get down the same way in reverse. Most people have a stronger side, so practise leading with each leg. Three to five times a day is a good starting point.

slides.title: Build the strength behind it
slides.body: Sit-to-stands from a chair, step-ups and lunges holding a bench all make floor transfers easier. Over a few weeks, try using less help from your hands.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: If you've had a fall, feel dizzy when you stand, or have knee, hip or back pain that stops you practising, get it assessed. A physio can adapt the steps for you.

caption:
Can you get down on the floor and back up again without a second thought?

It sounds simple, but it's a skill that combines strength, balance and confidence. Summer picnics, playing with the grandkids and floor stretches all rely on it, and practising it can make a slip less worrying.

Start with steps: roll to your side, onto hands and knees, into a half kneel, then push up, using a chair for support. Practise both ways and lead with each leg. Sit-to-stands and step-ups build the strength behind it.

story.headline: Floor to standing: try it today
story.body: Roll to your side, hands and knees, half kneel, then stand. Use a chair to start. Three times each side.
